Turing instabilities for three interacting species

Journal: arXiv
Vit Piskovsky Affiliation: Mathematical Institute, University of Oxford, Woodstock Road, Oxford, OX2 6GG, UK, vit.piskovsky@maths.ox.ac.uk
Abstract

In this paper, I prove necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of Turing instabilities in a general system with three interacting species. Turing instabilities describe situations when a stable steady state of a reaction system (ordinary differential equation) becomes an unstable homogeneous steady state of the corresponding reaction-diffusion system (partial differential equation). Similarly to a well-known inequality condition for Turing instabilities in a system with two species, I find a set of inequality conditions for a system with three species. Furthermore, I distinguish conditions for the Turing instability when spatial perturbations grow steadily and the Turing-Hopf instability when spatial perturbations grow and oscillate in time simultaneously.

Keywords: 
Turing instability , Turing-Hopf instability , reaction-diffusion systems , linear stability

1 Introduction

Assume that 𝐧∗\mathbf{n}^{*} is a unique stable steady state of the reaction system

d​ni​(t)d​t=fi​(𝐧​(t))\frac{\mathrm{d}n_{i}(t)}{\mathrm{d}t}=f_{i}(\mathbf{n}(t)) (1)

with species i=1,…,Ni=1,\dots,N of concentrations 𝐧=(n1,…,nN)\mathbf{n}=(n_{1},\dots,n_{N}). The linear stability of 𝐧∗\mathbf{n}^{*} as a steady state for the reaction-diffusion system

∂tni​(t,𝐱)=di​∂𝐱2ni​(t,𝐱)+fi​(𝐧⁡(t,𝐱))\partial_{t}n_{i}(t,\mathbf{x})=d_{i}\partial_{\mathbf{x}}^{2}n_{i}(t,\mathbf{x})+f_{i}(\mathbf{n}(t,\mathbf{x})) (2)

with species ii diffusing at rate di>0d_{i}>0 in the space 𝐱∈ℝN\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{N} is determined by the eigenvalues of the matrix

J⁡(k2)=J−k2​diag​(d1,…,dN),J(k^{2})=J-k^{2}\mathrm{diag}(d_{1},\dots,d_{N}), (3)

where the matrix J=∂𝐟/∂𝐧|𝐧∗J=\partial\mathbf{f}/\partial\mathbf{n}|_{\mathbf{n}^{*}} is the Jacobian for the reaction system (1) and, by assumption, has eigenvalues with negative real parts. We make the following definitions to analyze whether perturbation modes of wavelength kk can grow and oscillate.

Definition 1.

The spatially uniform steady-state 𝐧∗\mathbf{n}^{*} of (2) admits an instability if there is a wavenumber kk such that J⁡(k2)J(k^{2}) has an eigenvalue with a positive real part. Furthermore, if any eigenvalue of J⁡(k2)J(k^{2}) with a positive real part is real for any wavenumber kk, we call the instability a Turing instability. Otherwise, if some eigenvalues of J⁡(k2)J(k^{2}) with a positive real part are not real at some wavenumber kk, we call the instability a Turing-Hopf instability.

Importantly, a Turing instability corresponds to linearly growing perturbation modes, while a Turing-Hopf instability implies growing perturbation modes that oscillate. For a system with N=2N=2 species, it is well-known [1] that any instability must be a Turing instability and it occurs precisely when

J11​d2+J22​d1>2​d1​d2​det​J.J_{11}d_{2}+J_{22}d_{1}>2\sqrt{d_{1}d_{2}\mathrm{det}J}. (4)

For N=3N=3 species, both Turing and Turing-Hopf instabilities can occur and linear stability has been analysed for some restricted choices of the matrix JJ [2, 3] or diffusivities did_{i} [4]. Moreover, partial conditions that specify the existence of diffusivities did_{i} that give rise to instabilities for a fixed matrix JJ have been provided [5, 6].

    At least one of the roots has a negative real part.

By the fundamental theorem of algebra, the cubic function p⁡(λ)p(\lambda) has three complex roots, say λ1\lambda_{1}, λ2\lambda_{2} and λ3\lambda_{3}. Moreover,

To prove (c), notice that if two roots λ1\lambda_{1} and λ2\lambda_{2} have negative real parts and one root λ3\lambda_{3} is real positive, then either λ1=λ2¯∉ℝ\lambda_{1}=\overline{\lambda_{2}}\notin\mathbb{R} or λ1,λ2<0\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}<0. 4 Proof of the Main Result

To prove the main result, notice that the eigenvalues λ\lambda of J⁡(k2)J(k^{2}) in (3) are given by the characteristic equation

Definition 2.

If an eigenvalue λ\lambda crosses the boundary Re​λ=0\mathrm{Re}\lambda=0 at λ=0\lambda=0 (resp. pure imaginary value) for some k2>0k^{2}>0, then k2k^{2} is called a Turing value (resp. Turing-Hopf value).

For N=3N=3 species, the Turing (resp. Turing-Hopf) values characterise the Turing (resp. Turing-Hopf) instabilities.

Lemma 3.

The steady-state ni∗n_{i}^{*} of (2) with N=3N=3 species admits a Turing-Hopf instability if and only if there exists a Turing-Hopf value κ2\kappa^{2}. Moreover, it admits a Turing instability if and only if there exists a Turing value κ2\kappa^{2} and no value k2k^{2} is a Turing-Hopf value.

Proof.

Since instability occurs precisely when there exists a Turing or a Turing-Hopf value and the existence of a Turing-Hopf value implies a Turing-Hopf instability, it suffices to show that a Turing-Hopf instability implies the existence of a Turing-Hopf value. For a contradiction, suppose that there is a Turing-Hopf instability but not a Turing-Hopf value. Due to a Turing-Hopf instability, there is a complex conjugate pair of eigenvalues with positive real parts at some value κ2>0\kappa^{2}>0. By Lemma 1(a), the remaining eigenvalue at κ2\kappa^{2} is negative real. Since eigenvalues vary continuously with k2k^{2} and all eigenvalues have negative real parts for sufficiently small and sufficiently large k2k^{2}, the two eigenvalues that form a complex conjugate pair at κ2\kappa^{2} must cross the line Re​λ=0\mathrm{Re}\lambda=0 as k2k^{2} increases and decreases from κ2\kappa^{2}. Since there is no Turing-Hopf value, there are either (i) at least three distinct Turing values or (ii) two distinct Turing values and the pair of eigenvalues collides at these Turing values. In the case of (i), the product of eigenvalues c0​(k2)c_{0}(k^{2}) has at least three distinct positive roots corresponding to the Turing values. However, c0​(y)c_{0}(y) is a cubic with c0​(0)=a~0<0c_{0}(0)=\tilde{a}_{0}<0 and a negative leading coefficient, implying that it can admit at most two positive real roots. In the case of (ii), c0​(y)c_{0}(y) has two positive real roots that coincide with the two Turing values. Moreover, as a pair of eigenvalues crosses λ=0\lambda=0 at the Turing values, the product of the eigenvalues c0​(y)c_{0}(y) does not change a sign at the crossing. Consequently, the two Turing values are distinct positive roots and maxima of c0​(y)c_{0}(y), contradicting that the cubic c0​(y)c_{0}(y) can admit at most one positive maximum. ∎

Finally, as the signs of the leading and constant coefficients in (15) are fixed, Lemma 2 can be applied to the function g​(y)=c0​(y)g(y)=c_{0}(y) or to the pair of functions g⁡(y)=c2​(y)​c1​(y)−c0​(y)g(y)=c_{2}(y)c_{1}(y)-c_{0}(y) and h​(y)=c1​(y)h(y)=c_{1}(y). In particular, the main result in Theorem 1 follows if I prove the following two results in Lemma 4 and Lemma 5.

Lemma 4.

The steady-state 𝐧∗\mathbf{n}^{*} of (2) with N=3N=3 species admits a Turing-Hopf instability iff there is a value y′′>0y^{\prime\prime}>0 such that c1​(y′′)>0c_{1}(y^{\prime\prime})>0 and c2​(y′′)​c1​(y′′)−c0​(y′′)>0c_{2}(y^{\prime\prime})c_{1}(y^{\prime\prime})-c_{0}(y^{\prime\prime})>0.

Proof.

(⇒\Rightarrow) By Lemma 3, a Turing-Hopf instability implies the existence of a Turing-Hopf value κ2\kappa^{2} when a pair of complex conjugate eigenvalues λ=±i​ω∈i​ℝ∖{0}\lambda=\pm i\omega\in i\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\} exists. In particular, ω2​c2​(κ2)=c0​(κ2)\omega^{2}c_{2}(\kappa^{2})=c_{0}(\kappa^{2}) and ω2=c1​(κ2)\omega^{2}=c_{1}(\kappa^{2}), implying that c2​(κ2)​c1​(κ2)=c0​(κ2)c_{2}(\kappa^{2})c_{1}(\kappa^{2})=c_{0}(\kappa^{2}) and 0<c1​(κ2)0<c_{1}(\kappa^{2}). By Lemma 1(a), the remaining eigenvalue must remain negative in the neighbourhood of wavenumbers around κ\kappa. As kk crosses κ\kappa, the distribution of eigenvalues changes from three eigenvalues with negative real parts to a single negative eigenvalue and a complex conjugate pair of eigenvalues with a positive real part. Therefore, by Lemma 1(b), c2​(k2)​c1​(k2)−c0​(k2)c_{2}(k^{2})c_{1}(k^{2})-c_{0}(k^{2}) changes from negative to positive and c1​(κ2)c_{1}(\kappa^{2}) remains positive as kk crosses κ\kappa. Therefore, there must exist y′′>0y^{\prime\prime}>0 such that c1​(y′′)>0c_{1}(y^{\prime\prime})>0 and c2​(y′′)​c1​(y′′)−c0​(y′′)>0c_{2}(y^{\prime\prime})c_{1}(y^{\prime\prime})-c_{0}(y^{\prime\prime})>0.

(⇐\Leftarrow) By Lemma 1(d), the existence of y′′>0y^{\prime\prime}>0 such that c1​(y′′)>0c_{1}(y^{\prime\prime})>0 and c2​(y′′)​c1​(y′′)−c0​(y′′)>0c_{2}(y^{\prime\prime})c_{1}(y^{\prime\prime})-c_{0}(y^{\prime\prime})>0 implies that there is a complex conjugate pair of eigenvalues with a positive real part at k=y′′k=\sqrt{y^{\prime\prime}}, corresponding to a Turing-Hopf instability. ∎

It is worth remarking that, for N=3N=3 species, the existence of a Turing-Hopf instability not only ensures that there is a value κ2\kappa^{2} such that J⁡(κ2)J(\kappa^{2}) has a complex conjugate pair of eigenvalues with a positive real part but also that these eigenvalues have the largest real part (Lemma 1(a)), implying that the oscillatory growth of the perturbation mode with wavelength κ\kappa provides the dynamically dominant behaviour.

Lemma 5.

The steady-state 𝐧∗\mathbf{n}^{*} of (2) with N=3N=3 species admits a Turing instability iff it does not admit a Turing-Hopf instability and there is a value y′>0y^{\prime}>0 such that c0​(y′)>0c_{0}(y^{\prime})>0.

Proof.

(⇒\Rightarrow) By Lemma 3, a Turing instability implies the absence of a Turing-Hopf instability and the existence of a Turing value κ2\kappa^{2}. At κ2\kappa^{2}, one or two eigenvalues λ\lambda pass through λ=0\lambda=0, while at least one eigenvalue has a negative real part by Lemma 1(a). If two eigenvalues pass through λ=0\lambda=0 simultaneously, then the product of eigenvalues c0​(k2)c_{0}(k^{2}) remains unchanged at κ2\kappa^{2}, implying that κ2\kappa^{2} is a local maximum of c0​(k2)c_{0}(k^{2}) with c0​(κ2)=0c_{0}(\kappa^{2})=0. Since c0​(k2)c_{0}(k^{2}) is a cubic, κ2\kappa^{2} is a global maximum and c0​(k2)<0c_{0}(k^{2})<0 for any k2≠κ2k^{2}\neq\kappa^{2}. Consequently, there is no other Turing value. Since the two eigenvalues that cross into the region Re​λ>0\mathrm{Re}\lambda>0 must leave this region at sufficiently large and sufficiently small k2k^{2}, there must exist a Turing-Hopf value, contradicting the existence of a Turing instability due to Lemma 3. Therefore, only one eigenvalue can pass through λ=0\lambda=0. When this happens, the remaining two eigenvalues either have negative real parts or one is real positive and the other real negative. Consequently, there is a value y′=k2y^{\prime}=k^{2} in the neighbourhood of κ2\kappa^{2} such that there is one real positive eigenvalue and two eigenvalues with negative real parts. By Lemma 1(c), it follows that c0​(y′)>0c_{0}(y^{\prime})>0.

(⇐\Leftarrow) If there is a value κ2>0\kappa^{2}>0 with c0​(κ2)>0c_{0}(\kappa^{2})>0, then Lemma 1(c) implies that there is one real positive eigenvalue and two eigenvalues with negative real parts at κ2>0\kappa^{2}>0. As k2k^{2} decreases from κ2\kappa^{2}, some eigenvalue must pass through Re ​λ=0\textrm{Re }\lambda=0 since all eigenvalues have negative real parts for sufficiently small k2k^{2}. Moreover, at least one of the eigenvalues that pass through Re ​λ=0\textrm{Re }\lambda=0 must be real since the parity of real eigenvalues that pass through Re ​λ=0\textrm{Re }\lambda=0 must coincide with the parity of eigenvalues in the region Re ​λ>0\textrm{Re }\lambda>0 and there is one such eigenvalue at κ2\kappa^{2}. Therefore, there exists a Turing value. By Lemma 3, the existence of a Turing value and the absence of a Turing-Hopf instability implies the existence of a Turing instability. ∎

5 Conclusions

I derived the conditions for Turing patterns to form in a general reaction-diffusion system with three interacting species (Theorem 1). The Turing patterns form due to the instability of the homogeneous stationary state to spatial perturbations. I showed that the pertubations can either grow steadily (Turing instability) or with oscillations in time (Turing-Hopf instability) and analyzed when each instability type occurs (Theorem 1).
